Every one is a 120ms ease-out transition on the property that changes, and nothing else moves — no lift, no scale, no shadow. Hover is never the only signal: each of these also has the focus ring from 23a.

These were specified one at a time across seven documents, which is how a codebase ends up with four different greys. Three families: a surface warms (rows, chips, the dark and orange controls all move one step in the direction they already lean), ink darkens (tabs, footer links, text links), or orange appears where there was none (name links). Nothing changes size, position or elevation on hover — the table has 25 rows and a lift on each one turns scanning into a flicker.

24Narrow widths — every page type at 420px

Every spec has a "Narrow widths" paragraph and none of it was drawn, so the collapse rules were being read rather than seen. Five cards at 420px, the width where every rule has already fired: the board, the detail page, the scoring modal, the homepage and the by-month timeline. The principle in all five is that columns collapse in order of how much they carry — activity goes before handle, handle goes to a second line before the name truncates, and the two numbers a reader came for, rank and score, never move.

24cScoring modal at 420px

How contributor scores are tallied

Each action earns a base number of points, scaled by the issue/PR's priority label. Every point is then multiplied by a recency factor that decays over time, so recent work counts for more.

✕
BASE POINTS × PRIORITY × RECENCY = SCORE
1 · Base points
Opened an issue × PRIORITY1
Opened a PR × PRIORITY2
PR was merged × PRIORITY10
Issue resolved by a merged PR × PRIORITY4
2 · Priority — higher-priority work counts for more

Anything tagged × PRIORITY is scaled by the issue/PR's priority label (applied by maintainers). Work with no priority label stays at 1×. Confirmed issues add +2 on top for the person who opened them, up to a 5.5× cap.

P03.5× P13× P22.5× P32× P41.5× No priority label1×
3 · Recency — recent work counts for more

Every action fades over time. It's worth half as much after each 182-day half-life, and anything older than 365 days no longer counts. Monthly boards are not decayed.

1×Today
0.5×182 days
0.25×364 days
0×365+ days
Example

When a Priority: P1 PR you opened merges, the author merge bonus alone earns 10 base × 3× priority × 0.5× recency (≈6 months old) = 15 pts, on top of the points for opening it. The same work today, before any decay, would be worth twice as much.

10×3×0.5=15points

Same modal as 19b below ~820px. The grid collapses to one column in the order base points, priority, recency, example. The formula strip wraps. The decay bar keeps its four columns — the bars shrink, the labels do not wrap. Panel margin drops to 16px and the radius to 10px; header, copy and components are otherwise unchanged.

{{ byMonthH1 }}

Why group open {{ noun }} by month?

A long list of open issues can be daunting and discouraging. To make things more manageable, we group issues by the month they were last updated. This breaks the backlog into smaller, more approachable segments.

Developers can focus on a specific month—like issues from March—and make visible progress. Each update or resolution shortens the list, providing a clear sense of momentum and accomplishment.

This view also makes it easier to spot older issues that may have fallen through the cracks, giving the community an opportunity to reassess and take action where needed.

21Contributor Leaderboard — the link, and the length

Two fixes. The "How scoring works" link sits on its own line between the intro and the tabs, attached to nothing — it reads as a stray. It belongs at the end of the sentence that raises the question, where the reader is already thinking about scoring. Second, the board runs to hundreds of rows in one uninterrupted column: no count, no way to find yourself, no end in sight, and every row weighted the same as the one above it. The page gives a reader in 240th place no way to reach their own row except the scrollbar. Same data, made navigable: a header strip that says how many there are, a search, a jump-to-me control, the first 25 rows, and a count-anchored "Show more". Row density is tightened so 25 rows fit where 16 did.

20How scoring works — standalone page

The page stacks the contributor section on top of the maintainer section and prints the full multiplier stack inside each — the same six priority rows and four recency rows, twice. The multipliers are identical for both boards, so the duplication implies a difference that is not there, and the second board's actions sit a thousand pixels below the first. Content also runs at half the page width, leaving the right half empty all the way down. Rebuilt on 19a's parts: formula once at the top, the two boards side by side showing only what differs between them, and the shared multipliers stated once underneath where they visibly cover both.

20aBoards side by side, multipliers stated once
Magento Open Source Forger
Home Leaderboard Issues PRs
LFLaura Folco

How scoring works

Every contribution on the leaderboard earns points. Here's exactly how each board is scored — the base points per action, the multipliers that scale them, and an example. The rolling 12-month boards decay older work; the monthly boards do not.

BASE POINTS × PRIORITY × RECENCY = SCORE Same formula on both boards

Contributor board

ActionBase points
Opened an issue × PRIORITY1
Opened a PR × PRIORITY2
PR was merged × PRIORITY10
Issue resolved by a merged PR × PRIORITY4
Example

When a Priority: P1 PR you opened merges, the author merge bonus alone earns 10 base × 3× priority × 0.5× recency (≈6 months old) = 15 pts, on top of the points for opening it. The same work today, before any decay, would be worth twice as much.

10×3×0.5=15points

Maintainer board

ActionBase points
Approved a PR3
Requested changes on a PR3
Commented on a review1
Approved a PR that later merged × PRIORITY6
Claimed a stale pending-review PR2
Applied a triage label1
Example

When a Priority: P1 PR you approved later merges, the merge bonus alone earns 6 base × 3× priority × 0.5× recency (≈6 months old) = 9 pts, on top of the points for the approval itself. The same work today, before any decay, would be worth twice as much.

6×3×0.5=9points

Multipliers

Identical on both boards

Base points are multiplied together with the factors below. A multiplier of 1× leaves the score unchanged; higher values boost it.

Priority — higher-priority work counts for more

Anything tagged × PRIORITY is scaled by the issue/PR's priority label (applied by maintainers). Work with no priority label stays at 1×. Confirmed issues add +2 on top for the person who opened them, up to a 5.5× cap.

P03.5× P13× P22.5× P32× P41.5× No priority label1×
Recency — recent work counts for more

Every action fades over time. It's worth half as much after each 182-day half-life, and anything older than 365 days no longer counts. Monthly boards are not decayed.

1×Today
0.5×182 days
0.25×364 days
0×365+ days

14Issues / PRs by Month

The page renders 84 identical orange tiles. Every one is the same size and the same colour, so the only varying thing — the count — has no visual weight: 261 issues and 1 issue look alike, and "261 Issu…" truncates inside its box. The word "Issues" is repeated 84 times, the year totals sit in yellow at roughly 1.9:1 on white, and months with nothing in them are rendered as live tiles. 14bOne timeline — the backlog has a shape

{{ byMonthH1 }}

Why group open {{ noun }} by month?

A long list of open issues can be daunting and discouraging. To make things more manageable, we group issues by the month they were last updated. This breaks the backlog into smaller, more approachable segments.

Developers can focus on a specific month—like issues from March—and make visible progress. Each update or resolution shortens the list, providing a clear sense of momentum and accomplishment.

This view also makes it easier to spot older issues that may have fallen through the cracks, giving the community an opportunity to reassess and take action where needed.

13Chrome on a wide screen — contents in the content container

Shown at 1600px with the page content in a 1100px centred container, which is what the live site does. The dark bands and the hairline stay edge to edge; everything inside them is constrained to the same container, so the logo starts where the page content starts and the login button ends where it ends. Compare the screenshot: at 2560px, edge-anchored chrome puts the logo and the login button a screen's width away from anything they relate to, and the footer columns land against the right edge with a void beside them. The centre of the header looks emptier this way — that is the page's real measure, not a gap to fill.

12Footer on the 11a header spec

The current footer is a full-bleed orange band carrying one sentence and one button, then a dark strip of trademark text — roughly 280px of page to deliver a single link. With the masthead now dark and orange reduced to a hairline, a solid orange footer is the loudest thing on the page and contradicts the header. Both options below mirror the header: same #15171b, same orange hairline, same mono for secondary text. Orange survives only on the Slack button, so header and footer bookend the page identically. 8Highlights — UX pass

Problems with the current page: "first contribution →" is repeated ten times and "back after" twelve times, so the only varying part of each row (the number) is buried at the end of a sentence; the two panels have different header depths, so their first rows don't align; nothing is ranked or comparable; Comebacks is sorted by length of absence, which puts the least-engaged person first and runs on for a full screen; and the intro promises four categories — newcomers, fast risers, returning, active now — when the page shows two.
